RGC 2 · preprocessing study · working report

Choosing the intensity transformation for RGC 2

Seventeen candidate stretches, five label-free image tests and one fixed CNN probe, measured on 6249 real cutouts. The verdict: asinh beats linear S/N by +0.126 AUC on identical folds — and it wins for a reason that has nothing to do with information content.

Summary

RGC 1.0 inherited its preprocessing — per-image min–max scaling written out as an 8-bit PNG — rather than choosing it. Before RGC 2 freezes a data pipeline, the choice had to be made empirically on the actual cutouts: which intensity stretch, on which noise estimator, at which output geometry. This report covers the stretch.

Recommended pipeline 
FITS (float64, Jy/beam)
  → σ from the reflected negative half of the pixel distribution
  → z = (I − B) / σ
  → clip below 1σ                largest single lever (+0.044 AUC) — verify on BYOL first
  → asinh(z / 3)          a = 3–10 is a plateau; do not tune inside it
  → ÷ asinh(10⁴ / 3)             FIXED divisor — keeps absolute S/N comparable
  → crop to 3′ (FIRST/VLASS), full field (LoTSS)
  → anti-aliased resample
  → float32 .npy          never uint8
+0.126ΔAUC, asinh_a3 over snr_linear, 9/9 paired wins
0.124AUC spread among arms carrying identical information
×959 → ×6.5peak-S/N spread, before and after asinh
0.00%of 3–10σ pixels tied by the 1σ floor

1The physical problem the transformation exists to solve

A FIRST cutout arrives as a float64 array in Jy/beam: 150 × 150 px at 1.80″/px over a 4.5′ field, one beam spanning 2.78 px. The intensity range inside a single frame is brutal. The core or hotspot sits at 10²–10³σ above the background, while the structures that actually decide the morphological class — the jets and tails, their opening angle, their curvature, where they fade — sit at 3–10σ.

Across the sample the problem repeats at the population level. Measured over 400 frames per survey (03_stretch.py, block E), the peak S/N spans a factor of 959 on FIRST (4.2 → 4042) and 12 345 on VLASS (4.7 → 58 531). A network fed linear intensity therefore faces two simultaneous problems: within each image nearly all of the numeric range is consumed by a handful of core pixels, and across images the same physical brightness lands on wildly different numbers.

Why this is a morphology problem, not a cosmetics problem

WAT and NAT are separated by the opening angle of faint tails, not by anything the bright core does. Bending is the ram-pressure signature — P = ρv², where P is the pressure the intracluster medium exerts on the jets, ρ is the density of that medium and v the galaxy's speed through it — and the observable that encodes it lives in the faintest resolved emission in the frame. A representation that spends its range on the hotspot is spending it on the one part of the source that carries the least class information.

So the stretch is a decision about where to spend output range. That framing is what the whole study measures.

2Data

6249 sources with a FIRST cutout, each downloaded on a common 4.5′ field across five surveys but on five different pixel grids (00_audit.py). 5738 sources have all five.

* AllWISE frames are not a fixed size — 197 or 198 per axis with tile-edge truncations down to 169; only 39% match nominal. LoTSS is the weak link: 465 ids missing plus ~2% entirely NaN (outside the DR2 footprint).

The single most consequential row in Table 1 is the last column. The three radio surveys are ~50% negative — they are properly sky-subtracted, with noise centred on zero. That is what makes a source-free noise estimator possible (§3.1). AllWISE has no negative pixels at all: it is in DN with a pedestal, so the whole S/N framing has to be rebuilt for it, and it is excluded here along with DESI.

The labelled working set is 2076 FIRST sources — 750 WAT, 727 NAT, 409 sFRII, 190 sFRI — joined from the Lao, MiraBest and Sasmal parent catalogues.

Two prerequisites that had to be fixed first

The filename prefix is not the catalogue widx. The catalogue lists each sky position once per parent catalogue and the download merged those duplicates, so the prefix falls behind widx by a running count of duplicates — 0 at the start, 770 by the end. Settled from each cutout's own WCS (09_verify_ids.py): read as widx the median separation from the catalogue position is 104 885″ (29°) with 0.0% inside 5″; read as download-list position it is 0.72″, 100.0% inside 5″, and the provenance tag baked into the FIRST filename agrees 6249/6249. Joining on widx took the WAT-vs-NAT probe from AUC 0.774 to 0.504 — exactly chance. Every label-dependent number below was produced twice, before and after the fix.

The labels are provisional. The WAT/NAT flags come from single-survey classification in the parent catalogues; the programme's own multi-frequency policy — decide on FIRST, fix the vertex and core on VLASS, confirm extent and that the bend is real on LoTSS — has not been applied. Everything is therefore tagged label-independent (§5.1–5.5, safe now) or label-dependent (§5.6–5.7, provisional). As it turns out, the recommendation rests mostly on the label-independent tier.

3Method — the arms and the label-free tests

Notation used throughout

Every symbol is also glossed at the equation where it first appears; this panel is the single place to look them all up.

The image
I
Raw pixel intensity as it comes out of the FITS file. Units are Jy/beam for the three radio surveys, nanomaggy for DESI, DN for AllWISE.
B
Background level — the sky value the emission sits on, one number per frame, estimated by the chosen noise estimator.
σ
Noise rms, one number per frame. Also used as the unit in which everything faint is quoted: "a 5σ tail" means a pixel five noise-widths above background. Not to be confused with the softening scale a, which is measured in these same units.
z
Signal-to-noise map, eq. (1) — the background-subtracted image expressed in units of σ. Every stretch in this study is a function of z alone, so no arm can win by getting a different background or noise estimate.
zpk
Peak S/N of one frame, max(z) over that image — how bright the source's brightest pixel is relative to its own noise. Ranges from 4.2 to 4042 on FIRST.
y
Output pixel value — what the stretch produces and the network is actually handed. Different arms put y on different scales; that is the whole point of the comparison.
px/beam
Pixels spanning one telescope beam. Nyquist sampling needs ≥ 2; below that the instrument's own resolution is being thrown away by the pixel grid.
r99
Radius enclosing 99% of a source's flux — the size measure used to justify cropping.
Stretch parameters
a
Softening scale of the asinh stretch, in units of σ. The S/N at which compression switches on: below a the map is linear, above it logarithmic. The central tuning knob of this study.
zref
Fixed reference S/N — the constant divisor that maps to output 1.0, chosen near the top of the peak-S/N distribution (1000 in the probe, 10⁴ in the recommended pipeline). Being a constant rather than a per-frame quantity is what preserves absolute brightness across the sample. Distinct from zpk, which varies frame to frame.
f
Floor, in σ. Everything below f is clipped up to f before stretching: f = 1 for asinh_a3_floor1, f = 3 for sigclip3_mm.
γ
Exponent of the power-law arm, fixed at 0.25.
mm(·)
Per-image min–max operator, eq. (5) — rescale so this frame's own minimum is 0 and its maximum 1.
med, MAD
Median and median absolute deviation, scaled so that MAD equals σ for Gaussian noise (astropy's mad_std). Both are robust to bright outlier pixels, which is why they are used instead of mean and standard deviation.
Measured quantities and statistics
AUC
Area under the ROC curve — the probability that the classifier scores a randomly chosen WAT above a randomly chosen NAT. 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect. Threshold-free, which is why it is the headline metric here.
bal. acc.
Balanced accuracy — mean of the per-class recalls, so a classifier that always guesses the majority class scores 0.5 rather than being flattered by class imbalance.
S
Faint span, eq. (13) — the fraction of an arm's output range separating a 3σ feature from a 10σ one. The study's measure of "how much range goes to the tails".
R
Contrast ratio, eq. (14) — core brightness above the extended emission, divided by extended emission above background. High R means range is being spent on the hotspot.
Δ
Difference in AUC between two arms, computed run by run on matched splits.
dz
Paired effect size = mean(Δ) / sd(Δ). How large the gap is relative to its own run-to-run wobble; roughly, values above 1 mean the gap is bigger than the noise on it.
p
Two-sided paired t-test p-value over the 9 matched runs — the probability of seeing a gap this large if the two arms were really equivalent. Small means the difference is real; p ≈ 1 means the arms are indistinguishable.
s.e.m.
Standard error of the mean = sd / √n, the uncertainty on a reported average.
r
Correlation coefficient, −1 to +1. In Table 2 it is the correlation between a frame's estimated noise and its source size — a positive value means the estimator is being inflated by the source it is supposed to ignore.
rank corr
Spearman rank correlation between y and z. Exactly 1 means the arm preserves the complete ordering of pixel brightnesses, i.e. it is invertible and throws nothing away.
ties
Fraction of distinct z values that get mapped onto a shared output value — pixels the arm can no longer tell apart. Reported both over all pixels and restricted to the 3–10σ band.

3.1Normalising to units of the local noise

Every arm operates on the same S/N map, so the noise estimator is held fixed and only the stretch varies:

z= I − Bσ (1)

I is the raw pixel intensity from the FITS file (Jy/beam); B the background level of that frame, a single number; σ the noise rms of that frame, also a single number; and z the resulting signal-to-noise map — the same image expressed in units of its own noise, so that "3" means "three noise-widths above the sky" in every frame regardless of how the telescope was calibrated.

This is not cosmetic. A σ biased by the source itself propagates straight into the image the network sees, and if the bias tracks angular size it tracks the class. Six estimators were compared (02_estimator.py): whole-frame median + MAD, 3σ-clipped stats, an outer-10% border, an r = 0.35–0.5R annulus, a hybrid, and the reference —

B=med(I), σ=MAD( { I< } ∪ { 2B − I< } ),  I< = { I < B } (2)

med is the median over all finite pixels and MAD the median absolute deviation, scaled so it equals σ for Gaussian noise; both are used instead of mean and standard deviation because they are unmoved by a handful of very bright source pixels. I< is the set of pixels fainter than the median — the negative half of the distribution — and 2B − I< is that same set mirrored across the median to rebuild the positive side artificially. The union of the two is a symmetric distribution made entirely of pixels no source contributed to. { · } denotes a set of pixel values, and ∪ their union.

Equation (2) is the negative estimator: real emission is positive, so on a sky-subtracted interferometric map the negative half of the pixel distribution is essentially pure noise. Reflect it about the median and take the MAD, and the estimate is source-free by construction. It is the reference every other estimator is scored against, and it degrades gracefully to sigma-clipping where no negative half exists.

3.2The seventeen arms

rgc2pp/stretch.py defines seventeen arms with a common signature, all pure elementwise functions of z. They fall into four physical families, and the family — not the individual arm — is what carries the argument.

Family I — absolute, fixed divisor

These put the image in units of the local noise and divide by a constant, so a 20σ tail is the same number in every image and absolute surface brightness stays comparable across the sample. zref is fixed at roughly the top of the peak-S/N distribution.

ylin= zzref yasinh= asinh(z / a) asinh(zref / a) (3, 4)

y is the output value handed to the network; z the S/N map from eq. (1); zref a fixed constant — the same number for every image in the dataset — set near the top of the peak-S/N distribution so that a source at that brightness maps to output 1.0; and a the softening scale, in units of σ, which sets the S/N at which the compression begins. asinh is the inverse hyperbolic sine, asinh(x) = ln(x + √(x² + 1)). Dividing by asinh(zref/a) is what normalises the output to roughly 0–1 without ever consulting the individual frame.

Six arms: snr_linear, and asinh_a{1, 3, 10, 30, 100}. Note that snr_linear is the a → ∞ limit of (4), so the a-sweep and the linear baseline are one continuous family.

Family II — per-image relative

These rescale by something measured in the frame itself, usually the brightest pixel. They discard absolute surface brightness — the standard defence against a network clustering on flux instead of morphology — but they make the faint-structure budget hostage to the hotspot.

y= y′ − min y′ max y′ − min y′ , y′ ∈ { z, asinh(z/a) } (5)

y′ is whatever intermediate map is being rescaled — either the S/N map z itself, or an already-stretched version of it — and min y′, max y′ are the smallest and largest values within that one frame. That is the defining property of the family: the divisor is measured from the image at hand, so two frames are rescaled by different amounts and their brightnesses are no longer comparable. ∈ means "is one of".

Seven arms: minmax_f32, minmax_u8 (RGC 1.0's behaviour, (5) followed by 8-bit quantisation), zscore, zscale (IRAF limits, clipped both ends), pct_clip (0.5–99.5 percentile), asinh_a3_mm, asinh_a30_mm.

Family III — one-sided compressive

y=√(z+/zref) y= ln(1+z+) ln(1+zref) y=(z+/zref)γ (6–8)

z+ = max(z, 0) is the S/N map with every negative pixel forced to zero — these three functions are undefined or badly behaved on negative input, so the clip is not optional. √ is the square root, ln the natural logarithm (base e), the 1 + z+ inside it keeps the logarithm finite at zero, and γ is the power-law exponent, fixed at 0.25. zref is the same fixed constant as in eq. (3)–(4).

Three arms: sqrt, log, power_g0.25. The clip is the point of interest — from Table 1, it destroys roughly half of every frame.

Family IV — floored / denoising

y=mm( asinh(max(z, f) / a) ), f = 1 y=mm( max(z, f) − f) , f = 3 (9, 10)

f is the floor, in units of σ — the S/N below which everything is treated as noise and flattened. max(z, f) raises every pixel fainter than f up to exactly f, so they all become the same number and the noise texture disappears; subtracting f in eq. (10) then puts that flattened floor at zero. mm(·) is the per-image min–max operator of eq. (5), which is what makes these two arms per-image rather than absolute. a is the softening scale as before.

Two arms: asinh_a3_floor1 and sigclip3_mm. The second is the workhorse of the radio-morphology ML literature — everything below a few sigma set to zero so the network cannot learn the noise. It is lossy by construction; the question is what it loses.

3.3What asinh actually does, analytically

Before any measurement, the functional form already predicts the behaviour, and it is worth writing down because the empirical optimum turns out to sit exactly where the algebra puts it. asinh has two limits,

asinh(x) ≈ x  (x ≪ 1),  asinh(x) ≈ ln(2x)  (x ≫ 1) (11)

x stands for the argument z/a, i.e. a pixel's S/N measured in units of the softening scale. ≪ and ≫ mean "much smaller than" and "much larger than", and ≈ "is approximately". So the two lines read: for pixels well below a the function is a straight line, and for pixels well above it the function is a logarithm. a is the crossover between the two regimes, which is exactly why it is the parameter worth tuning.

so a is literally the S/N at which compression switches on. Below a the map is linear in z — noise is neither amplified nor suppressed, and the noise floor keeps its symmetry. Above a it is logarithmic, folding decades of core brightness into a small range. The gradient makes the range allocation explicit:

dydz = 1 a · asinh(zref/a) · √(1 + (z/a)²) (12)

dy/dz is the derivative of the output with respect to the input — in plain terms, how much output range one extra unit of S/N buys you at that brightness. It is the quantity the whole argument turns on. The √(1 + (z/a)²) in the denominator is what makes it fall off: at low z the bracket is ≈ 1 and the gradient is flat (every faint pixel is treated alike), while at high z it grows in proportion to z and the gradient collapses. The constant a · asinh(zref/a) is just the fixed normalisation from eq. (4) and does not depend on the pixel.

Output range per unit S/N therefore falls as 1/z once z ≫ a. Evaluating (12) at a 5σ tail pixel against a 200σ core pixel: at a = 3 the tail gets 34× more range per unit S/N than the core, at a = 10 it gets 18×, at a = 100 only 2.2×, and linear gives exactly 1× by definition. That ratio is the entire mechanism.

Combining (4) and (11) gives a closed form for the quantity the study measures as faint span — the fraction of an arm's own range separating a 3σ feature from a 10σ one:

S(a) = asinh(10/a) − asinh(3/a) asinh(zpk/a) (13)

S(a) is the faint span written as a function of the softening scale. The numerator is the output distance between a 10σ pixel and a 3σ pixel — the two ends of the band where WAT and NAT tails live — and the denominator is the arm's full output range, set by the brightest pixel in the frame at zpk. The ratio is therefore the share of the available range that the faint band gets, a pure number between 0 and 1. The literal 3 and 10 are the σ levels bounding the band, not free parameters. Note zpk here, not zref: the span is a property of one frame.

S(a) has an interior maximum. For a frame with peak S/N of 49 (the FIRST median) it peaks at a* = 3.6; at peak 215 it peaks at a* = 2.6; at peak 1000, at a* = 2.1. Small a wastes range compressing the noise floor itself; large a reverts to linear and re-concentrates range on the core. The algebra predicts an optimum near a ≈ 2–4 before a single network is trained — hold that against §5.7.

3.4The label-free test battery

Five tests measure properties of the image. None of them touches a class label, which is what makes them safe to act on now.

Test C — range budget (03_stretch.py, 400 frames/survey). The measured version of (13): locate the pixel closest to 3σ and to 10σ, and report their output separation as a fraction of the arm's own range. Affine-invariant, so arms with different divisors compare fairly.

Test D — the a-sweep (400 frames, per class). The metric is a dimensionless contrast ratio over three masks, each a set of pixels selected on the same z map:

  • core = {z > 0.5zpk} — pixels brighter than half the frame's own peak, i.e. the hotspot or the core.
  • extended = {3 < z < 0.1zpk} — pixels above the 3σ detection threshold but below a tenth of the peak: the jets, lobes and tails.
  • background = {z < 1} — pixels below 1σ, which is sky.

The thresholds are written relative to zpk so that the same three masks mean the same thing on a bright source and a faint one.

R= ⟨y⟩core − ⟨y⟩ext ⟨y⟩ext − med(y)bg (14)

⟨y⟩core is the mean output value over the core mask, ⟨y⟩ext the mean over the extended-emission mask, and med(y)bg the median over the background mask — median rather than mean there because the background is where outliers do most damage. Angle brackets ⟨·⟩ denote an average over the pixels in a mask. The three masks are defined on z, not on y, so every arm is scored over the same physical pixels. Numerator = how far the core sits above the jets and lobes; denominator = how far those sit above the sky. In the invariance statement, α is any rescaling and β any offset — dividing one difference by another cancels both, which is what lets a fixed-divisor arm and a per-image arm be compared on one axis.

R is invariant under y → αy + β. That matters: the earlier bench min–max renormalised each arm before measuring, which silently undid the fixed-divisor property it was meant to test. Low R means the arm spends its range on the tails rather than the hotspot. Reported per class, because the FR-II hotspot risk and the WAT/NAT tail benefit live in different classes.

Test E — fixed divisor viability. Does a single global zref work, or must every image be min–maxed? Measured as the ratio of maximum to minimum peak output across the sample, before and after the stretch.

Test N — what the one-sided arms discard. The fraction of pixels below 0σ and below 1σ.

The information audit (11_information.py, 250 FIRST frames). Three quantities per arm: the Spearman rank correlation between y and z; the tie fraction, i.e. the fraction of distinct z values mapped onto a shared output value; and the effective number of 8-bit levels available. Crucially, ties are computed twice — over all pixels, and restricted to the 3–10σ band. That second column is what separates discarding noise from discarding signal.

Quantisation (08_quantisation.py, 400 frames/survey). Round-trip error of the stretch in float32 and of min–max in uint8, both expressed back in σ units, plus the effective level count inside the 3–10σ band.

4Method — the CNN probe

The label-free tests can show that an arm hands more numeric range to faint structure. They cannot show that a network uses it. That third channel — inductive bias — needs a classifier, and the classifier has to be an instrument rather than a model: fixed, small, and identical across arms so that the only varying factor is the stretch.

4.1Architecture

Not ConvNeXT and not DSteerableLeNet — in the papers' model numbering those are M1 and M2, where M1…M6 label the six architectures benchmarked in Paper I and M2 is RGC itself. This is instead a purpose-built probe, Probe in 05_probe.py:101: 

input          1 × 96 × 96 float32
4 × block      Conv2d 3×3 (bias=False) → BatchNorm2d → ReLU → MaxPool2d(2)
   widths      16 → 32 → 64 → 96
head           global average pool → Linear(96, 2)
parameters     ≈ 110 000

Small enough to train seventeen times on a CPU, large enough that the ranking is not noise-limited. Augmentation is a random element of D4, the eight-element symmetry group of the square: a rotation by k × 90° with k ∈ {0,1,2,3}, followed by a horizontal flip with probability ½. This is the group the real E(2)-equivariant RGC network is built to respect — E(2) being the group of rotations, reflections and translations of the plane — so the probe is not rewarding an arm for accidental orientation cues.

4.2Protocol

  • Task. WAT vs NAT on FIRST, balanced by subsampling to 727 per class (1454 images). Chosen deliberately: it is the well-powered split, and it is the one that should be stretch-sensitive, since the classes differ in the opening angle of faint tails rather than in the bright core. If the stretch matters anywhere, it matters here.
  • Order of operations. The arm is applied at native 150 px, then resampled to 96 px with anti-aliasing. The stretch acts on measured surface brightness, so it belongs before any resampling — which is also the order a deployed pipeline would use.
  • Estimator held fixed. z is cached once with sigclip (04_zcache.py) and every arm is applied to that same cached map through an identity patch, so no arm can win by getting a different σ.
  • Splits. StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0). Every arm sees the identical split-and-seed grid, so runs are paired — the only way to compare two arms whose difference is smaller than the fold-to-fold spread.
  • Optimisation. AdamW at a learning rate of 3 × 10⁻³ (the step size taken at each update) with weight decay 10⁻⁴ (a penalty on large weights), a OneCycle learning-rate schedule, 30 epochs — one epoch being one pass over the training fold — batch size 64, and cross-entropy loss. Per-fold standardisation subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation of the training fold only, so no test information leaks in.
  • Metrics. ROC-AUC and balanced accuracy on the held-out fold. Sweep at 3 folds × 2 seeds; the top seven arms re-run at 3 folds × 3 seeds with per-run values retained for paired t-tests and win counts.
Instrument checks — does the probe measure what it claims?

Bent vs straight: AUC 0.820. WAT vs NAT on an earlier pilot run: 0.774. The same probe on the mis-joined widx labels: 0.504 — exactly chance. It responds to real signal and collapses to chance when the signal is destroyed, which is the behaviour an instrument should have.

5.1Noise estimator label-free

Correlation between σ inflation and source extent — the size coupling that would turn a noise estimate into a class proxy — plus the median ratio to the source-free reference:

Estimator size-coupling, 02_estimator.py. corr is the correlation between the σ an estimator returns and how much of the frame the source covers: positive means the estimator is being inflated by the very source it is meant to ignore, and since angular size differs between classes, that inflation would leak class information into the normalisation. ratio is the estimator's σ divided by the source-free reference σ from eq. (2); 1.000 would be perfect agreement.
estimatorcorr FIRSTcorr VLASScorr LoTSSratio LoTSS
median_mad reject+0.447+0.393+0.9251.038
sigclip−0.201+0.352+0.6931.006

On FIRST and VLASS the estimator barely matters — every method lands within 1–4% of the source-free reference and the class-conditional bias is under 0.3%. On LoTSS it matters a great deal: median_mad (RGC 1.0's behaviour) is almost perfectly size-coupled at r = +0.93 — a correlation of 0.93 out of a possible 1.0 between the noise it reports and the size of the source in the frame, which means it is measuring the source, not the sky. annulus is unusable — a ring at 0.35–0.5R is not source-free, it collects neighbours, and on LoTSS returns σ up to 26× the truth.

The premise behind the earlier recommendation also fails outright. The worry was that large bent sources inflate their own noise. In fact WAT and NAT are the smallest classes on sky — median fraction of the FIRST frame above 3σ: sFRI 1.57%, sFRII 1.07%, WAT 0.95%, NAT 1.04%. The straight FR sources are the extended ones. Decision: negative for the radio surveys, sigclip acceptable on FIRST/VLASS; never median_mad, never annulus.

5.2The information audit — the result that needed no labels label-free

This test reframed the entire question. minmax, zscore, snr and asinh at every a are strictly monotone functions of z. A monotone map is invertible, so they carry identical information.

Table 3. Information audit, 250 FIRST frames (11_information_vla.csv). The decisive column is ties on 3–10σ, not the rank correlation.

minmax_f32, zscore, snr_linear1.00000.00%0.00%27lossless

asinh_a31.00000.00%0.00%47lossless
asinh_a10 / a30 / a1001.00000.00%0.00%43 / 33 / 28lossless

Read the last two columns, not the first. Clipping the noise floor and clipping faint signal are different operations that both register as "ties." asinh_a3_floor1 ties 82.8% of all pixels but 0.00% of the 3–10σ pixels where the WAT/NAT signal lives — it discards noise and nothing else. zscale ties only 0.6% overall but 24.5% of the faint band — it discards structure. A single global tie rate would have ranked those two the opposite way round.

What this establishes

The stretch cannot be justified on information-preservation grounds, because among Family I arms there is nothing to preserve differently. It can only matter through three channels: (i) ties on faint signal — irreversible, and this rules out pct_clip, zscale and minmax_u8; (ii) precision, which only bites at 8 bits (§5.5); and (iii) inductive bias — how readily a network picks faint structure up, which is unmeasurable without labels and a fixed architecture (§5.6).

5.8What it looks like

The tables say the arms differ. These figures say how, and two of them show something the tables cannot.

5.9A negative result worth recording

10_labelfree.py attempted to rank the arms without labels, using between-source against within-source (nuisance) variance ratios. It does not work, and it is kept as a warning. Two defensible-looking variants — an all-pixel Fisher ratio and one restricted to faint pixels — rank the arms almost inversely to each other: minmax_f32 scores J = 63.4 (rank 1 of 17) on the first and Jfaint = 77.8 (rank 4) on the second, while asinh_a1 scores 8.4 (rank 15) and 101.2 (rank 1). minmax tops both overall because per-image divisor differences inflate between-source scatter with brightness, which is not morphology.

This is not a fixable detail. Among information-equivalent arms there is nothing for such a statistic to measure, so any number it reports is a property of its own pixel weighting. Neither variant feeds the recommendation.

6Discussion

6.1Why asinh beats linear — the mechanism, in three parts

The headline comparison is asinh_a3 0.8015 against snr_linear 0.6755: Δ = +0.126, 9/9 paired wins, p < 10⁻⁶, with balanced accuracy falling from 0.724 to 0.582 — barely above chance. These two arms share the same z map, the same fixed divisor zref, the same information content (rank correlation exactly 1, zero ties anywhere) and the same network. The only difference is the compression, so the mechanism must be entirely in how range is allocated. Three measurements pin it down.

(i) Within-image allocation. Equation (12): at a = 3 a 5σ tail pixel receives 34× more output range per unit S/N than a 200σ core pixel; linear gives it 1×. Measured, that is Table 4 — the faint band occupies 21.3% of the range under asinh_a3 against 10.4% under linear on FIRST, and 16.4% against 2.6% on LoTSS.

(ii) Across-image comparability. Table 6: the ×959 population spread in peak S/N becomes ×6.5 after asinh. This is the part that is easy to miss. Because the probe standardises the whole dataset with a single mean and standard deviation, an uncompressed fixed-divisor arm leaves most frames sitting near zero while a few dominate the scale entirely — the ×959 spread arrives undigested. The fixed divisor is safe because asinh collapses the spread first, not on its own. That is why snr_linear — the one arm keeping absolute S/N without compressing it — is last by a wide margin, and it is the single most useful causal statement in the study.

(iii) The noise floor survives. Below z = a asinh is linear (eq. 11), so the noise keeps its symmetric, sky-subtracted character — roughly half of every frame, untouched. That is what separates asinh from sqrt, log and power, which achieve similar range budgets (Table 4) but clip half the frame and score 0.808, 0.774 and 0.712 respectively.

6.2The largest single finding is not about asinh

Channel 3 dominates

The information-preserving arms — formally interchangeable, rank correlation exactly 1, zero ties anywhere — span 0.687 to 0.811 AUC. That 0.124 spread among representations that carry the same information is entirely inductive bias, and it dwarfs everything the information audit can see. The stretch is worth choosing carefully, but for optimisation reasons, not information ones.

This inverts the usual framing. The literature argument for asinh is that it is information-preserving; §5.2 shows that is true but vacuous, because the linear baseline it is compared against is equally information-preserving. The real argument is that a network trained by gradient descent on a finite dataset is not invariant to monotone reparameterisation of its input, and the size of that non-invariance here is 0.124 AUC.

6.3a is a plateau, not a peak

Unpaired: 0.766 (a=1) → 0.801 (3) → 0.805 (10) → 0.772 (30) → 0.731 (100) → 0.687 (linear). Paired, a = 3 against a = 10 gives Δ = +0.0022, p = 0.61, 5/9 — a coin flip. Do not tune a inside 3–10.

The agreement between the two independent routes to this number is the strongest internal check in the study. Equation (13) put the analytic optimum at a* = 2.1–3.6 across the observed peak-S/N range, purely from the functional form; the range-budget measurement put the FIRST maximum at a = 3; and the classifier, which knows nothing about any of that, puts it at 3–10. Physically the plateau is bounded on both sides: below a ≈ 1 the compression begins inside the noise floor and starts amplifying noise texture (visible directly in asinh_a1, Figure 5), and above a ≈ 30 the map is asymptotically linear again and re-concentrates range on the core.

6.4The awkward result: the lossy arms do well

asinh_a3_floor1, zscale and sigclip3_mm take the top three, and sigclip3_mm has a rank correlation of 0.18 with z — it destroys almost all of the ordering and still scores 0.822. Discarding sub-threshold noise evidently helps this probe more than the information it costs. Two distinct things are going on, and §5.2 is what tells them apart.

asinh_a3_floor1 and sigclip3_mm discard only the noise floor — their ties on 3–10σ pixels are 0.00%. Their alarming global tie rates (82.8%, 98.9%) are entirely sub-threshold. zscale is the genuine anomaly: it destroys a quarter of the faint ordering and still reaches tier 2, presumably because saturating the core removes brightness variation the network would otherwise key on — a benefit a properly normalised model should not need, and which comes bundled with the visible core saturation in Figures 4 and 7. It should not be adopted on this evidence.

The 1σ floor is worth +0.044 AUC over plain asinh_a3 (9/9, 95% CI [+0.036, +0.051]), and §5.2 shows it costs nothing in faint signal. It is the largest single lever measured. It is also the one recommendation carrying real risk — see §6.7.

6.5What RGC 1.0's asinh benefit really was

Table 7 forces a re-reading of the earlier pipeline. RGC 1.0 wrote min–max to 8-bit PNG, so any comparison of "asinh vs min–max" in that setting confounded two changes: the nonlinearity, and the abandonment of the 8-bit step. Separating them, the 8-bit step alone costs 0.120σ of round-trip error on FIRST and 0.408σ on LoTSS, and cuts the faint band from 48 levels to 26 (FIRST) or from 43 to 8 (LoTSS). Much of the apparent benefit of asinh in RGC 1.0-style pipelines is really the 8-bit step being avoided — the two were never separated. Consistently, minmax_u8 and minmax_f32 score identically on the probe (0.762 both), because at 96 px input on a 110k-parameter CNN the precision channel is not the binding constraint; it is the range allocation that is.

6.6Corrections to the earlier bench

Recorded so the superseded conclusions are not rebuilt on.

6.7Limitations

  • Provisional labels. Everything in §5.6–5.7 rests on single-survey parent-catalogue flags. Label noise that is independent of the arm attenuates every arm's score roughly equally, so the ranking should survive while the absolute AUCs are floors, not estimates.
  • One task, one survey. WAT vs NAT on FIRST alone. If the eventual class is assigned from a multi-survey view, the preprocessing that best serves a FIRST-only classifier is not automatically the one that serves the classifier we will actually build.
  • One architecture, and a small one. 110k parameters trained from scratch on 1454 images is capacity- and data-limited, which is exactly the regime where noise suppression acts as regularisation. That is the specific reason the 1σ floor cannot be adopted on this evidence: self-supervised objectives frequently rely on the noise realisation as the thing augmentations contrast against, so under BYOL the effect may invert.
  • DESI and AllWISE are untested. Both are audited but neither has been through the stretch or probe blocks, because neither is sky-subtracted the way the radio maps are. AllWISE in particular has no negative pixels, so equation (2) and the whole S/N framing need rethinking before either can be included.
  • The crop is unvalidated by the probe. §5 geometry results support a 3′ crop for FIRST/VLASS on source-size grounds (median r99 = 25.5″ on a 135″ field), but it changes px/beam and has not been run through the probe.

7Recommendation

Ranked by what each choice is worth on the probe: asinh over linear +0.126, 1σ floor +0.044, the value of a inside 3–10: +0.000.

Adopt
  • negative estimator (eq. 2) on the radio surveys; sigclip acceptable on FIRST/VLASS. Never median_mad, never annulus.
  • asinh(z/a) with a = 3, and no further tuning inside 3–10.
  • A fixed divisor asinh(zref/a), preserving absolute S/N. Viable only in combination with asinh (§6.1 ii).
  • float32 .npy output. Never uint8 (§5.5).
  • Anti-aliased resampling, always. Crop to 3′ on FIRST/VLASS, full field on LoTSS.
Adopt only after one more test

The 1σ floor. It is the largest single lever (+0.044, 9/9) and it provably costs no faint signal (0.00% ties on 3–10σ). But it was measured on a small CNN trained from scratch, where suppressing noise acts as regularisation. Test it on the real BYOL-pretrained model, with and without, before it goes into the pipeline. Fallback if it misbehaves: asinh_a3 with no floor, which costs 0.044 here and is unconditionally information-preserving.

8Open items

  1. Re-run the probe sweep on the multi-frequency labels once they exist. Expect absolute AUCs to rise; watch whether the four tiers hold. Re-run on multi-survey input as well, not FIRST alone.
  2. BYOL floor test (§7). The one open question that could change the recommended pipeline.
  3. DESI and AllWISE. Build a per-band background and noise model appropriate to a crowded optical field, decide between a per-band stretch and a colour-preserving Lupton et al. (2004) asinh composite (stretch.lupton_rgb, implemented but untested), then re-run §5.2 and §5.6 on them.
  4. Geometry decisions. No single output grid preserves both VLASS and DESI — their beams need 270 and 1030 px over 4.5′, so decide between per-survey encoder stems and downsampled channels. AllWISE needs WCS reprojection, not plain resize (max offset 20.5″, and its frames vary in shape). Decide a LoTSS availability policy: drop the 465 missing plus ~2% NaN sources, or make LoTSS an optional channel with a presence flag.
  5. Confirm the crop through the probe — cheap, and it changes px/beam.
  6. Then build the dataset: run the chosen pipeline over all 6249 sources, write float32 .npy per survey, and record the estimator, stretch and geometry parameters alongside so the preprocessing is reproducible from the manifest rather than from memory.
